editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech adds one concrete thing to the Prime Minister's devolution pitch: an offer of 'DWP devolution', meaning localised employment support shaped by Holyrood. Alongside it, Westminster is exploring handing innovation, enterprise and employability funding to Scotland's regions. This partly answers the worry that the offer goes over Edinburgh's head. The employment powers on the table would go to the Scottish Government first. Whether they ever reach Lanarkshire or Dundee would then be Holyrood's decision, not Downing Street's.

The policy rests on an anecdote. A 2023 visit to one Easterhouse project became Greater Manchester's Live Well model. The speech says only that 'it worked' and achieved 'more than we could have imagined'. It offers no figures, then proposes taking the model 'nationwide', 'not a project on one estate'. British public policy has many bottom-up pilots that shone because of local leadership and committed staff, and then faded when they were turned into national programmes. The 'names not numbers' principle needs numbers of its own before it is scaled up.

The figure worth watching is the one the speech admits is shared with England: around one in six young people in Scotland are not in education, employment or training. That is the measure against which devolved employment support should be judged in a few years. Speeches about tick-box systems and Poverty Safari are not.

The Ravenscraig passage is a fair diagnosis. A steelworks closed by people 'hundreds of miles away', and its site was still being filled more than thirty years later. But the cure on offer is mostly about administrative structures. Lanarkshire did not decline because it lacked an employability budget. It declined because the industry left. The reindustrialisation half of the speech is thinner: shipbuilding, Grangemouth, a £10 million pair of defence colleges, and a call for buy-British procurement. Without that half, devolving the means to manage decline is not the same as reversing it.
